## 1. What you'll build, and why

Concurrency's great hazard is the **data race**: two tasks touching the same mutable state at once,
corrupting it. Swift's answer is the **actor** — a reference type that *serializes* access to its
state, so only one task touches it at a time. The remarkable part is *how* Swift guarantees it: not
with locks you might forget, but at **compile time**. You cannot even write the racy code — the type
checker rejects a synchronous reach into an actor from outside, demanding `await` (a hop onto the
actor's executor) instead.

This concept builds that. An `actor` is, at runtime, just a class (concept 25's machinery — a heap
object with methods). The whole feature is one rule in the **type checker**: cross-actor access must
be `await`ed. That single rule is what makes concurrent Swift data-race-free *by construction*.

- **You implement:** the actor-isolation rule — reject a synchronous, non-awaited call to an actor
  method from a nonisolated context.
- **Outcome:** actors run and match `swiftc`; synchronous cross-actor access is a compile error with
  `swiftc`'s wording.

> **New to actors?** An `actor` looks like a class, but its mutable state is *isolated*: code outside
> the actor can't touch it directly. To call an actor's method from outside you write
> `await someActor.method()` — the `await` marks that you might *suspend* while the actor finishes
> whatever it's doing, then your call runs with the actor to itself. One-at-a-time access, enforced.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Isolation is a compile-time rule

![Actor isolation. An actor's state is reachable from outside ONLY through `await` — a hop onto the actor's executor, which serializes access. A synchronous call is a compile error: "actor-isolated … in a synchronous nonisolated context." Inside the actor, self-access is direct. A regular class has no isolation. The runtime is the class machinery; the value of actors is the compile-time guarantee.](figs/actors.png)

Here is the entire rule. A call `a.method()` where `a` has actor type is **isolated** — only legal
from a context that's allowed to touch the actor's state:

- **Inside the actor** (you're executing one of the actor's own methods, so `current_class` is the
  actor): synchronous access is fine. `self.balance += n` just works; calling another of the actor's
  methods is a plain call.
- **Outside the actor** (a nonisolated context — top-level code, a different type's method): you may
  only reach in with **`await`**. `await a.method()` is the *hop*: it suspends if the actor is busy,
  runs your call when the actor is free, and resumes you. A bare `a.method()` is a **compile error**.

So the checker needs three facts at a call to `a.method()`: is `a`'s type an actor? are we under an
`await`? are we inside that actor? If actor-and-not-awaited-and-not-inside, reject. That's `TODO(39)`
— a few lines, and it's the heart of Swift concurrency safety.

### Tracking "are we under `await`?"

The one piece of state the rule needs is whether the call sits under an `await`. We add an `in_await`
flag: checking `Await e`'s operand sets it true (and restores it after). So in `await a.method()`,
when we reach the `Method_call`, `in_await` is true and the call is allowed; in a bare `a.method()`,
it's false and we reject. (We also track `current_class` — already there from classes — to allow
synchronous access *inside* the actor.) The set of actor names is collected up front from the
declarations.

### An actor is a class at runtime

Everything else — the `actor` keyword, the heap object, the `init`, the methods, dynamic dispatch —
**reuses concept 25's class machinery**. We parse `actor X { … }` exactly like `class X { … }`
(setting an `is_actor` flag), and lower it identically: `Alloc_ref`, a vtable, method dispatch. The
only divergence is in the type checker. This is faithful to swiftc: an actor *is* a reference type;
its special-ness is the isolation the compiler enforces, plus (in a real runtime) the serial
executor it runs on.

### Why our runtime serialization is "free" (the honest part)

In real Swift, the *runtime* enforcement of "one task at a time" is the actor's **serial executor** —
a queue that runs the actor's submitted work one item at a time, even on a multi-threaded global
executor. Our executor (concept 38) is **single-threaded and cooperative**, so there's no true
parallelism to serialize against — the runtime serialization is automatic and degenerate. That's why
this concept's *value* is the **compile-time rule**, not a runtime queue. The honest framing: we
build the part that makes actors *safe* (the type rule, which is real and matches swiftc), and note
that the runtime queue-hop a concurrent executor needs is the same `await`-suspend mechanism from
concept 38, here trivial.

> Oracle: `swift/lib/Sema/TypeCheckConcurrency.cpp` (the `ActorIsolation` checker — `SE-0306`);
> `SerialExecutor` in `_Concurrency`. The diagnostic we match — *"call to actor-isolated instance
> method '…' in a synchronous nonisolated context"* — is swiftc's, near-verbatim.

## 3. Build it, step by step

In `sema.ml`, in the `Method_call` handler's `TClass cn` case, add the isolation check. Given:
`actors` (the set of actor names), `in_await` (true under an `await`), `current_class` (the type
whose method we're checking), and `m`/`span`. Emit
`err span "call to actor-isolated instance method '%s' in a synchronous nonisolated context"` when
**all three** hold: `Hashtbl.mem actors cn`, `not !in_await`, and `!current_class <> Some cn`. Then
fall through to the normal method lookup. Reference: `solution/sema.ml`. Run with
`make lab C=phase8-arm64-backend/39-actors`.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase8-arm64-backend/39-actors
```

cram: an actor (a `Bank`) runs and matches `swiftc` through awaited deposits/withdrawals; a
synchronous non-awaited actor call is rejected with `swiftc`'s wording; inside-actor access is
synchronous and a regular `class` is unaffected. alcotest: the sync call is rejected, the awaited
call accepted, inside-actor access accepted, and a plain class is never isolated.

## 5. Benchmark it

There's nothing new to time — actors run as classes, and the isolation rule is a type-check-time
check. The conceptual "benchmark" is the *guarantee*: an entire class of concurrency bug (the data
race on shared mutable state) is made *unrepresentable*, at zero runtime cost beyond the executor
hop. That's the trade compile-time concurrency safety makes — and why Swift, Rust, and others invest
in it.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Property isolation.** Extend the rule to actor *property* access (`a.balance` from outside is
   isolated too), not just methods — `swiftc` rejects both.
2. **`nonisolated`.** A `nonisolated func` on an actor (that touches no isolated state) is callable
   synchronously from anywhere. Parse the keyword and exempt those members from the rule.
3. **`Sendable` checking (lite).** A value crossing an actor boundary must be `Sendable` (safe to
   share). Flag passing a non-`Sendable` (e.g. a mutable class) into an actor call.
4. **Global actors (`@MainActor`).** A type or function pinned to a global actor; calls between the
   `@MainActor` context and others follow the same await rule. Track a "current global actor."
5. **The real runtime hop.** On the concept-38 executor, make `await a.method()` actually enqueue on
   a per-actor serial queue (re-entrancy-aware), so two tasks awaiting the same actor genuinely
   serialize — the runtime half that's degenerate in our single-threaded model.

## 7. Recap & what's next

An `actor` serializes access to its state, and Swift enforces it at **compile time**: cross-actor
access must be `await`ed (a hop onto the actor's executor); inside the actor it's synchronous. At
runtime an actor is a class; the value is the type rule — a few lines in the checker that make data
races unrepresentable. We match `swiftc`'s behaviour and its diagnostic.

Next, the course's capstone: **40-macros** — a compile-time AST→AST **macro expander** that runs
*before* sema, the final piece of the front end (and a survey of modules / incremental compilation).
With it, the project — a complete Swift compiler subset, two backends — is done.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

```ocaml
(* in the Method_call handler's `TClass cn` case — the actor-isolation rule *)
| Types.TClass cn -> (
    if Hashtbl.mem actors cn && (not !in_await) && !current_class <> Some cn then
      err span
        (Printf.sprintf
           "call to actor-isolated instance method '%s' in a synchronous nonisolated context" m);
    match Option.bind (Hashtbl.find_opt classes cn) (fun cl -> Types.vsig cl m) with
    | Some (ptys, ret) -> check_args (Printf.sprintf "method '%s'" m) ptys; ret
    | None -> err span (…); …)
```

The given pieces: the actor set + the `in_await` flag (set while checking `Await`'s operand), and
`actor` parsed/lowered as a class.

```ocaml
let actors : (string, unit) Hashtbl.t = Hashtbl.create 8 in
List.iter (function Ast.IClass c when c.Ast.is_actor -> Hashtbl.replace actors c.Ast.cname () | _ -> ())
  prog.Ast.items;
let in_await = ref false in
…
| Ast.Await (e0, _) ->
    let saved = !in_await in in_await := true;
    let t = infer e0 in in_await := saved; t
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — property isolation
Apply the same three-condition check in the `Member` (property read) and `Set_member` (property
write) handlers when the base type is an actor: reject `a.balance` / `a.balance = …` from a
nonisolated, non-awaited context. swiftc isolates the whole stored-property surface, not just methods.

### 2 — nonisolated
Add a `nonisolated` keyword on a member; record the nonisolated method names per actor. In the rule,
skip the check when `m` is nonisolated. (swiftc additionally verifies a `nonisolated` member touches
no isolated state — a stricter check you can add.)

### 3 — Sendable (lite)
Mark `Int`/`Bool`/`String`/value types `Sendable`; classes (mutable reference types) not. At an actor
call, check each argument's type is `Sendable` and flag the rest — the data that crosses the boundary
must be safe to share, which is the deeper reason actors are race-free.

### 4 — global actors
`@MainActor` pins code to one shared actor. Track a `current_global_actor`; a call from `@MainActor`
to a non-`@MainActor` function (or vice versa) follows the await rule. It's the same isolation check
with a global, rather than instance, identity.

### 5 — the real runtime hop
Give each actor a serial queue (a list of pending closures) and a "busy" flag. `await a.method()`
checks the flag: if free, run directly and mark busy; if busy, enqueue the continuation and yield
(concept 38). When a method finishes, dequeue the next. Now two tasks awaiting the same actor
genuinely serialize — the runtime guarantee that, on our single-threaded executor, was free.
```
